title: Proximity-induced charge transfer, strain and magnetic exchange in graphene/CrSBr heterostructure
authors: Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Niraj Aryal, Turgut Yilmaz, Margalit L. Feuer, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Abhay Pasupathy, Xavier Roy, Jerzy T. Sadowski, Elio Vescovo
abstract: Stacking van der Waals materials provides a powerful route to engineer emergent electronic and magnetic behaviors through proximity-driven interactions. The graphene/CrSBr heterostructure has emerged as a compelling platform in this frontier, exhibiting exotic macroscopic responses-- including uniaxial surface-plasmon-polariton propagation and an unconventional quantum Hall effect-- indicative of strong interfacial electronic and magnetic coupling. However, a microscopic electronic landscape governing these phenomena has remained elusive. Here, we provide a comprehensive spectroscopic characterization of the graphene/CrSBr interface using a combination of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM), and density functional theory. We resolve a massive redistribution of interfacial charge that concurrently hole dopes graphene and populates the quasi-one-dimensional spin-polarized conduction band of CrSBr, resulting insulator-to-metal transition in the interfacial CrSBr layer. Furthermore, electronic structure of CrSBr exhibits strong momentum-dependent renormalization distinct from conventional charge doping, and theoretical modeling supported by Raman spectroscopy points to additional interfacial compressive strain. In addition, ARPES reveals a splitting-like feature in the graphene Dirac cone consistent with spin degeneracy lifting, providing possible evidence of magnetic proximity coupling. These findings provide crucial microscopic insight into the system's optical and transport responses and establish graphene/CrSBr as a versatile platform for charge-transfer control, strain-driven band engineering, magnetic-proximity coupling, and directionally confined excitations for next-generation spintronic and nanophotonic devices.
summary: This work provides a comprehensive spectroscopic and theoretical investigation into the graphene/CrSBr interface. Researchers demonstrate that strong interfacial coupling causes significant charge transfer and electronic reconstruction, leading to novel properties like an insulator-to-metal transition and evidence of magnetic proximity effects. These findings establish the system as a versatile platform for next-generation spintronic devices.
main_problem: To microscopically understand the electronic landscape governing emergent behaviors, such as unconventional quantum Hall effects, in the graphene/CrSBr heterostructure driven by proximity interactions.
main_result: The interface exhibits massive charge redistribution leading to hole doping of graphene and an insulator-to-metal transition in interfacial CrSBr, alongside evidence for magnetic proximity coupling via Dirac cone splitting.
method: A combination of Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES), Low-Energy Electron Microscopy (LEEM), and Density Functional Theory (DFT) was employed to characterize the interface.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the graphene/CrSBr van der Waals heterostructure, investigating how interfacial charge transfer, strain, and magnetic coupling modify the electronic structure of both components.
key_observables: Interfacial charge redistribution, spin-polarized conduction band population, insulator-to-metal transition, splitting feature in the Dirac cone, and compressive strain effects.
important_parameters: The study investigates phenomena under various doping/strain conditions, focusing on electronic structure renormalization distinct from conventional doping.
main_assumptions: DFT calculations are used to provide qualitative insight into band alignment and strain trends, while experimental measurements map the actual electronic reconstruction at the interface.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	ext{CrSBr}$ structure, ARPES spectra along high symmetry paths, DFT-calculated bulk/interface electronic structures, and Fermi surface maps showing charge transfer effects.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting exotic responses in the heterostructure. It then presents spectroscopic characterization (ARPES/LEEM) to map the interfacial electronic state, supported by DFT calculations that model charge transfer, strain, and magnetic coupling mechanisms.
why_interesting: The strong focus on proximity effects, band engineering via external stimuli (strain, doping), and emergent magnetism in 2D van der Waals heterostructures is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron behavior in artificial quantum materials.
